criteria.text: Given the Command Center, when it is opened, then every tab is reachable and every card drills down one level.
Given sample mode, when any tab is shown, then the sample data is visibly labelled as sample.

Given the Command Center, when any tab renders, then .colaberry/plan.json and .colaberry/progress.json are both committed in this repo and every tab reads its content from them at runtime rather than from hard-coded values.
Given the Command Center, when any tab is shown, then .colaberry/manifest.json is committed in this repo and every tab shows how old that data is and warns when the age exceeds a week.
Trust — no tab shows a number, a connection or a result the project has not actually produced.

stories.notes: Nine tabs, every card drills to a detail page; all content read at runtime through assets/js/data.js. The published plan.json has no requirements, measures, guardrails or systems and placeholder dates, so those tabs show empty states and Overview > Plan check lists the gaps; plan.json was not edited. The Data model tab renders a proposal from knowledge/data-model.json and looks requirement statements up in plan.json. Run `npm test` (23 tests).

criteria.text: Given a new work order, when I create it, then it should appear in the system with GIS data.
Given an existing work order, when I update it, then the changes should be saved and reflected in the GIS data.
Trust: Given any work order action, when it is performed, then an audit trail entry must be created.

stories.notes: Verified against a STAND-IN GIS (server/gis/stand-in-assets.json): no access to the city GIS yet. The real GIS plugs in behind createGisClient() with the same getAsset/linkWorkOrder methods. Create, update and complete each write their audit entry in the same transaction; GIS write-back is queued in gis_sync and retried if GIS is down. Run `npm test` and `npm run demo`.

Given a GIS update, when processed, then the work order reflects the changes.
Trust: All GIS interactions are logged with timestamps.

stories.notes: Verified against the STAND-IN GIS (no city GIS access yet). Work order -> GIS: queued write-back from STORY-001. GIS -> work order: processGisChanges() polls numbered changes, applies each with its audit entry and cursor in one transaction. Every GIS call goes through createGisClient, which requires a logger and writes one gis_log row per attempt. Credential comes only from GIS_TOKEN; unauthorized is not retried. The demo reads the stand-in directly for display only. Run `npm test` and `npm run demo`.

criteria.text: Given the system's database, when accessed by Madison AI engines, then it should allow indexing and searching of work order data.
Given a request from Madison AI, when it queries the API, then it should receive the correct data format.
Trust: Given any data access by Madison AI, when it occurs, then it must be logged in the audit trail.

stories.notes: Madison AI reaches work order data through an audited, read-only HTTP API (list, changes-since, search, get one) rather than direct database access, as agreed with the student, so every access can be logged. Proven against our published OpenAPI contract and a SIMULATED Madison AI crawler; Madison AI's own spec and credentials are not available yet. Fails closed: no audit entry means no data. Run `npm test` and `npm run demo:api`.

stories.notes: Locate tickets from Blue Stakes are imported, updated, answered and completed, each audited in the same transaction. Verified against a STAND-IN Blue Stakes feed and client with PLACEHOLDER response codes; no Blue Stakes access yet. Exposed as API endpoints that need the locate_tickets:write scope; refusals are audited. Per-person logins come with STORY-007. Also fixed a flaky STORY-011 test (tests/madisonApi.test.js). Run `npm test` and `npm run demo:tickets`.
